title: Numeric Types and Ranges
learningObjectives: Explain the purpose and behavior of numeric types and ranges in C#.
Choose an appropriate type for a simple application scenario.
Read and explain original C# code that demonstrates the lesson concepts.
Predict deterministic program output and identify common mistakes.
Compile and execute a small .NET 10 console example to verify the result.

understand.concept: C# provides signed and unsigned integral types, plus float, double and decimal. Each type has a range and precision. Literal suffixes help select a type, and checked or unchecked contexts control how integral overflow is handled.
understand.whyItMatters: Correct numeric types prevent range errors, preserve intended precision and make calculations predictable.
understand.analogy: Numeric types are like measuring tools with different scales and capacities.
understand.analogyLimit: A wider range does not automatically mean more decimal precision. Floating-point types are approximate, while decimal is designed for decimal-based precision.

explain.narrative:
## Integral types

C# integral types include sbyte, byte, short, ushort, int, uint, long, ulong and nint/nuint. Each has a defined range. Use int for many ordinary counts, long for larger ranges and byte for small non-negative values when appropriate.

## Floating-point and decimal

float and double use binary floating-point and are appropriate for many scientific or measurement calculations. decimal provides higher base-10 precision and is commonly useful for financial amounts. No type should be selected solely because it is larger.

## Literals and boundaries

Suffixes such as L, U, F and M can make literal types explicit. MinValue and MaxValue expose integral boundaries. A checked integral operation throws on overflow; an unchecked operation follows the language's wraparound behavior for the relevant operation.

## Baseline

All examples target .NET 10 and C# 14.

examples.title: Inspect an integer range
examples.explanation: int exposes its smallest and largest representable values through MinValue and MaxValue.

examples.title: Use a long literal
examples.explanation: The L suffix makes the literal a long. Digit separators improve readability without changing the value.

examples.title: Compare numeric categories
examples.explanation: The F and m suffixes select float and decimal. A double literal is the default floating-point literal.

examples.title: Read byte boundaries
examples.explanation: byte is an unsigned 8-bit integral type with a range from 0 through 255.

examples.title: Detect checked overflow
examples.explanation: The checked expression throws when the int result is outside its representable range.

questions.prompt: Which C# type is designed for decimal-based financial precision?
questions.explanation: decimal is commonly selected for monetary values because of its base-10 precision model.

questions.prompt: What is the maximum value of byte?
questions.explanation: byte is an unsigned 8-bit type with values from 0 through 255.

questions.prompt: Which suffix makes an integer literal a long?
questions.explanation: The L suffix identifies a long integer literal.

questions.prompt: What does checked do for an integral overflow?
options: It converts the result to double
questions.explanation: A checked integral operation throws when the result is outside the type's range.

questions.prompt: Which statement about double is correct?
options: It stores every decimal fraction exactly
questions.explanation: double is a 64-bit binary floating-point type and many decimal fractions are approximations.
